Multiple passes of frontier AI render the text as close to the originals as possible. All work, data, and translation decisions are transparent and are published at the highest level of free and open possible.

canon.selection_help: Choose the canon your church uses, or see every available book with clear tradition labels. You can change this anytime.

Genesis.author: Anonymous; traditionally attributed to Moses. Modern scholarship sees a long compositional history with sources later edited together.
Genesis.audience: Israel in covenant identity, anchoring the people's origin story in God's creation, election, and promise.
Genesis.date: Composed across centuries; reached its received form c. 6th–5th century BC during/after the Babylonian exile.
Genesis.summary: Genesis tells of creation, humanity's rebellion and scattering, and the family of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph through whom God's covenant promises to Israel begin.

Exodus.author: Anonymous; traditionally attributed to Moses. Modern scholarship sees a long compositional history with sources later edited together.
Exodus.audience: Israel as a freed-and-covenanted people, learning what it means to be the LORD's nation under his law.
Exodus.date: Composed across centuries; reached its received form c. 6th–5th century BC.

Leviticus.author: Anonymous; traditionally attributed to Moses. Modern scholarship places it in the Priestly source.
Leviticus.audience: Israelite priests and the worshipping community — instructions for sacrifice, holiness, and the ordering of life around God's presence.
Leviticus.date: Compositional layers from the late monarchy through the post-exilic period (c. 7th–5th century BC).

Numbers.author: Anonymous; traditionally attributed to Moses.
Numbers.audience: Israel in transit between Egypt and the promised land — the wilderness generation, and later readers learning from their failures.
Numbers.date: Compositional layers from the late monarchy through the post-exilic period (c. 7th–5th century BC).

Deuteronomy.author: Anonymous; presented as Moses' farewell speeches. Modern scholarship anchors a core in the late 7th-century BC reform under Josiah.
Deuteronomy.audience: Israel preparing to enter the land — and later, exiles asking how to live faithfully without temple or king.
Deuteronomy.date: Core c. late 7th century BC; reached final form in the exilic period.

Joshua.author: Anonymous; part of the Deuteronomistic History.
Joshua.audience: Israel under the monarchy and exile, reflecting on conquest, covenant, and the meaning of the land.
Joshua.date: Compiled c. 7th–6th century BC from older traditions.

Judges.author: Anonymous; part of the Deuteronomistic History.
Judges.audience: Later Israel reading its pre-monarchic past as a cautionary cycle of apostasy and deliverance.

Ruth.author: Anonymous.
Ruth.audience: Post-exilic Israel — possibly arguing for inclusion of foreigners against exclusivist policies of Ezra-Nehemiah.
Ruth.date: Most likely post-exilic, c. 6th–4th century BC.

1 Samuel.author: Anonymous; part of the Deuteronomistic History.
1 Samuel.audience: Israel reflecting on the rise of the monarchy under Samuel, Saul, and David.
1 Samuel.date: Compiled c. 7th–6th century BC from older sources.

2 Samuel.author: Anonymous; part of the Deuteronomistic History.
2 Samuel.audience: Israel reading David's reign — its triumphs and tragedies — as the founding pattern of kingship.

1 Kings.author: Anonymous; part of the Deuteronomistic History.
1 Kings.audience: Exilic and post-exilic Israel, asking why the kingdom fell.
1 Kings.date: Reached final form during the Babylonian exile, c. 6th century BC.

2 Kings.author: Anonymous; part of the Deuteronomistic History.
2 Kings.audience: Exilic Israel — a theological autopsy of the divided kingdoms ending in Babylonian conquest.
2 Kings.date: Reached final form c. 6th century BC, after 586 BC.

1 Chronicles.author: Anonymous; tradition names "the Chronicler."
1 Chronicles.audience: Post-exilic Judean community in Persian-period Yehud, re-anchoring identity around David, the temple, and worship.

22.title: Solomon Chosen to Build God's House

Ezra.author: Anonymous; possibly the same hand as Chronicles.
Ezra.audience: Returnees rebuilding Jerusalem under Persian rule.

Nehemiah.author: Anonymous; incorporates a first-person memoir attributed to Nehemiah.
Nehemiah.audience: Returnees rebuilding Jerusalem's walls and renewing covenant under Persian rule.

Esther.author: Anonymous.
Esther.audience: Diaspora Jews under foreign rule, especially in Persia.
Esther.date: c. late Persian or early Hellenistic period (4th–3rd century BC).

Job.author: Anonymous.
Job.audience: Israelites wrestling with innocent suffering and divine justice.
Job.date: Wisdom-tradition consensus places the book c. 6th–4th century BC, drawing on older folk material.

Psalms.author: Multiple authors across centuries; superscriptions name David, Asaph, Korah, Solomon, Moses, and others.
Psalms.audience: Israel and the temple congregation in worship — and every later community of prayer and lament.
Psalms.date: Composed c. 10th–3rd century BC; final compilation in the post-exilic period.

Proverbs.author: An anthology; superscriptions name Solomon, Agur, Lemuel, and "the wise."
Proverbs.audience: Young Israelites being formed in wisdom for daily life.

Ecclesiastes.author: Anonymous; the speaker is "Qohelet," traditionally identified with Solomon.
Ecclesiastes.audience: Israelites confronting the limits of wisdom, wealth, and effort under the sun.
Ecclesiastes.date: Likely c. 5th–3rd century BC based on Aramaic-influenced Hebrew.

Song of Solomon.author: Anonymous; the superscription invokes Solomon.
Song of Solomon.audience: Israel reading erotic love as a lens on covenant intimacy — and later, Jewish and Christian readers reading it allegorically.

Isaiah.author: Multiple authors over centuries; chapters 1–39 root in 8th-century Isaiah of Jerusalem, while 40–55 ("Second Isaiah") and 56–66 ("Third Isaiah") respond to exile and return.
Isaiah.audience: Judah under Assyrian threat, Babylonian exile, and post-exilic restoration — successively.
Isaiah.date: Composed across c. late 8th to 5th century BC.

Jeremiah.author: Jeremiah of Anathoth; substantial editing by his scribe Baruch and later hands.
Jeremiah.audience: Judah on the eve of, during, and after the Babylonian conquest.

Lamentations.author: Anonymous; tradition attributes it to Jeremiah.
Lamentations.audience: Judeans grieving the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC.

Ezekiel.author: Ezekiel, an exiled priest in Babylon; with editorial development.
Ezekiel.audience: Judean exiles in Babylon, re-imagining God's presence apart from the temple.
Ezekiel.date: c. 593–571 BC for the prophet's ministry; final form somewhat later.

Daniel.author: Anonymous; presents itself as Daniel of the exile.
Daniel.audience: Jews under Hellenistic persecution — especially under Antiochus IV Epiphanes (167–164 BC).
Daniel.date: Reached its received form c. 165 BC; chapters 1–6 incorporate older court tales.

Hosea.author: Hosea ben Beeri.
Hosea.audience: The northern kingdom of Israel in its final decades before Assyrian conquest.

Joel.author: Joel ben Pethuel.
Joel.audience: Post-exilic Judah responding to a locust plague as a sign of the Day of the LORD.

Amos.author: Amos of Tekoa, a Judean shepherd preaching in the north.
Amos.audience: Northern Israel during a period of prosperity and injustice under Jeroboam II.

Obadiah.author: Obadiah.
Obadiah.audience: Judah after Edom betrayed Jerusalem — a prophecy of Edom's downfall.

Jonah.author: Anonymous; the protagonist is Jonah ben Amittai.
Jonah.audience: Post-exilic Israel — a satirical rebuke of ethnic insularity and an affirmation of God's mercy to outsiders.

Micah.author: Micah of Moresheth.
Micah.audience: Judah in the late 8th century BC, especially its rural poor against urban elites.

Nahum.author: Nahum of Elkosh.
Nahum.audience: Judah celebrating the impending fall of Nineveh.

Habakkuk.author: Habakkuk.
Habakkuk.audience: Judah confronting the rise of Babylon — a prophet's dialogue with God about justice.

Zephaniah.author: Zephaniah ben Cushi.
Zephaniah.audience: Judah under Josiah, on the eve of his reforms.

Haggai.author: Haggai.
Haggai.audience: Returnees rebuilding the temple under Darius.

Zechariah.author: Zechariah ben Berechiah; chapters 9–14 likely from a later hand.
Zechariah.audience: Returnees rebuilding the temple, and later post-exilic communities.
Zechariah.date: Chapters 1–8 c. 520–518 BC; 9–14 perhaps a century later.

Malachi.author: Anonymous; "Malachi" means "my messenger."
Malachi.audience: Post-exilic Judah growing lax in worship and faithfulness under Persian rule.

Matthew.author: Anonymous; tradition attributes it to the apostle Matthew. Modern scholarship sees a Greek-speaking Jewish-Christian author drawing on Mark and a Q-like source.
Matthew.audience: A Jewish-Christian community wrestling with continuity and discontinuity with synagogue Judaism.

Mark.author: Anonymous; tradition links it to John Mark, traveling companion of Peter.
Mark.audience: A Greek-speaking Christian community, possibly in Rome, under or near the threat of persecution.
Mark.date: c. 65–75 AD, around the Jewish War and the destruction of the temple.

Luke.author: Anonymous; tradition attributes it to Luke, traveling companion of Paul.
Luke.audience: A literate Greco-Roman Christian readership, addressed to "Theophilus."

John.author: Anonymous; tradition attributes it to the apostle John or the "Beloved Disciple."
John.audience: A Christian community in tension with synagogue Judaism, formed around the Beloved Disciple's witness.
John.summary: John presents Jesus as the eternal Word who reveals the Father, gives life through trust in him, and is glorified through his signs, death, and resurrection.

Acts.author: Anonymous; same author as Luke.
Acts.audience: A Greco-Roman Christian readership; second volume of the work addressed to Theophilus.

Romans.author: Paul, with the scribe Tertius.
Romans.audience: Christians in Rome — Jewish and Gentile believers in tension over Torah and identity.

1 Corinthians.author: Paul, with Sosthenes.
1 Corinthians.audience: The fractious Christian assembly in Corinth.

2 Corinthians.author: Paul, with Timothy.
2 Corinthians.audience: The Corinthian assembly, after a painful conflict.

Galatians.author: Paul.
Galatians.audience: Christian assemblies in Galatia (central Anatolia) being pressured to adopt circumcision and Torah observance.

Ephesians.author: Paul, or a close disciple writing in Paul's name (debated).
Ephesians.audience: A general Asian-Christian readership; the place name "Ephesus" is absent in the earliest manuscripts.
Ephesians.date: c. 60s AD if Pauline; c. 80s–90s AD if pseudonymous.

Philippians.author: Paul, with Timothy.
Philippians.audience: The Christian assembly at Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia.

Colossians.author: Paul, with Timothy — or a close disciple in Paul's name (debated).
Colossians.audience: Christians in Colossae in the Lycus valley, facing a syncretistic teaching.
Colossians.date: c. 60–62 AD if Pauline; later if pseudonymous.

1 Thessalonians.author: Paul, with Silvanus and Timothy.
1 Thessalonians.audience: The young Christian assembly at Thessalonica, facing persecution.
1 Thessalonians.date: c. 50–51 AD — likely the earliest surviving Pauline letter.

2 Thessalonians.author: Paul (debated; some scholars hold it pseudonymous).
2 Thessalonians.audience: The Thessalonian assembly, addressing eschatological confusion.

1 Timothy.author: Paul, or a disciple writing in Paul's name (the Pastoral Epistles are widely held pseudonymous).
1 Timothy.audience: Timothy as Paul's delegate at Ephesus; a guidance manual for later church order.
1 Timothy.date: c. mid-60s AD if Pauline; c. 90–110 AD if pseudonymous.

2 Timothy.author: Paul, or a disciple in Paul's name.
2 Timothy.audience: Timothy — framed as Paul's farewell from prison.
2 Timothy.date: c. mid-60s AD if Pauline; c. 90–110 AD if pseudonymous.

Titus.author: Paul, or a disciple in Paul's name.
Titus.audience: Titus as Paul's delegate on Crete.
Titus.date: c. mid-60s AD if Pauline; c. 90–110 AD if pseudonymous.

Philemon.author: Paul, with Timothy.
Philemon.audience: Philemon, a Christian slaveholder, regarding his runaway slave Onesimus.

Hebrews.author: Anonymous. Tradition has named Paul, Apollos, Barnabas, Priscilla, and others; no proposal commands consensus.
Hebrews.audience: Greek-speaking Jewish Christians tempted to drift back from their Christian confession.

James.author: Traditionally James the brother of Jesus; modern scholarship is split between authentic and pseudonymous attribution.
James.date: c. 50s–60s AD if authentic; c. late 1st century AD if pseudonymous.

1 Peter.author: Traditionally the apostle Peter, with Silvanus as scribe; some scholars hold it pseudonymous.
1 Peter.audience: Christians in Roman Asia Minor undergoing social hostility.
1 Peter.date: c. 60s AD if Petrine; c. 70s–90s AD if pseudonymous.

2 Peter.author: Traditionally Peter; widely held by modern scholarship to be pseudonymous.
2 Peter.audience: Christians facing scoffers who deny the parousia.

1 John.author: Anonymous; traditionally the apostle John or the Johannine elder.
1 John.audience: Johannine community after a schism, defining who belongs.

2 John.author: "The elder."
2 John.audience: A specific Christian assembly ("the elect lady") warned against false teachers.

3 John.author: "The elder."
3 John.audience: Gaius, an individual leader hosting traveling missionaries.

Jude.author: Traditionally Jude, brother of James and of Jesus.
Jude.audience: Christian communities being infiltrated by libertine teachers.

Revelation.author: John of Patmos (distinct in style from the Fourth Gospel).
Revelation.audience: Seven Christian assemblies in Roman Asia Minor under imperial pressure.
Revelation.date: c. 90s AD, traditionally during Domitian's reign.

Tobit.author: Anonymous.
Tobit.audience: Diaspora Jews navigating piety, marriage, and providence under foreign rule.
Tobit.date: c. 225–175 BC; composed in Aramaic with a Hebrew version also attested at Qumran.

Judith.author: Anonymous.
Judith.audience: Jews under foreign threat — a defiant story of pious resistance.

Greek Additions to Esther.author: Anonymous; supplementary material added in the Greek translation of Esther.
Greek Additions to Esther.audience: Greek-speaking Jews wanting an Esther story with explicit prayer and divine reference.

Wisdom of Solomon.author: Anonymous; pseudonymously attributed to Solomon. Composed in Greek by a Hellenistic Jewish author, likely in Alexandria.
Wisdom of Solomon.audience: Hellenistic Jews engaging Greek philosophy, defending Israel's wisdom against pagan and apostate alternatives.

Sirach.author: Yeshua ben Eleazar ben Sira of Jerusalem; Greek translation by his grandson.
Sirach.audience: Young Jewish men being trained in wisdom in Hellenistic-period Jerusalem.
Sirach.date: Hebrew original c. 195–175 BC; Greek translation c. 132 BC.

Baruch.author: Anonymous; pseudonymously attributed to Baruch, scribe of Jeremiah.
Baruch.audience: Diaspora Jews reflecting on exile, repentance, and wisdom.

1 Maccabees.author: Anonymous, likely a Jerusalem author writing in Hebrew (only the Greek survives).
1 Maccabees.audience: Jews under and after the Hasmonean revolt, narrating the legitimacy of the Hasmonean dynasty.

2 Maccabees.author: An anonymous epitomizer of a longer work by Jason of Cyrene; composed in Greek.
2 Maccabees.audience: Greek-speaking diaspora Jews — emphasizing martyrdom, providence, and resurrection.

1 Esdras.author: Anonymous; a Greek recomposition reordering 2 Chronicles 35–36, Ezra, and Nehemiah 7–8.
1 Esdras.audience: Hellenistic-period Jews wanting a clean narrative of return and restoration.

Prayer of Manasseh.author: Anonymous; pseudonymously attributed to King Manasseh.
Prayer of Manasseh.audience: Penitents identifying with Manasseh's repentance — used liturgically in some traditions.

Psalm 151.author: Anonymous; pseudonymously attributed to David. A Hebrew form is attested in 11QPsa.
Psalm 151.audience: Diaspora and Qumran communities devoted to David's psalter.

3 Maccabees.author: Anonymous; composed in Greek.
3 Maccabees.audience: Greek-speaking diaspora Jews of Egypt — a deliverance narrative set under Ptolemy IV.
3 Maccabees.date: c. 1st century BC to 1st century AD.

4 Maccabees.author: Anonymous; a Greek-speaking Jewish author influenced by Stoic philosophy.
4 Maccabees.audience: Hellenistic Jews — a philosophical sermon on reason mastering passion through faithfulness.

Bel and the Dragon.author: Anonymous; one of the Greek Additions to Daniel.
Bel and the Dragon.audience: Greek-speaking Jews — a mocking polemic against idolatry.

Letter of Jeremiah.author: Anonymous; pseudonymously attributed to Jeremiah.
Letter of Jeremiah.audience: Diaspora Jews tempted by surrounding idolatry.

Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three.display_name: Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three
Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three.author: Anonymous; one of the Greek Additions to Daniel.
Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three.audience: Greek-speaking Jews — liturgical material for Daniel 3.

Susanna.author: Anonymous; one of the Greek Additions to Daniel.
Susanna.audience: Greek-speaking Jews — a story of righteousness and false witness rebuked.

1 Clement.author: Anonymous, attributed to Clement of Rome.
1 Clement.audience: The Christian assembly at Corinth, embroiled in a leadership dispute.

1 Enoch.author: Anonymous; pseudonymously attributed to the antediluvian patriarch Enoch. A composite work assembled from several distinct sections.
1 Enoch.audience: Jewish apocalyptic communities reflecting on cosmic evil, judgment, and the calendar; later read in early Christian circles.
1 Enoch.date: Sections compiled c. 3rd century BC – 1st century AD; preserved in full only in Ge'ez (Ethiopic).

2 Baruch.author: Anonymous; pseudonymously attributed to Baruch, scribe of Jeremiah.
2 Baruch.audience: Jews after the destruction of the temple in 70 AD, processing exile theologically.
2 Baruch.date: c. late 1st – early 2nd century AD; preserved primarily in Syriac.

2 Esdras.author: Anonymous, with a Christian-edited frame around an originally Jewish core (4 Ezra, chapters 3–14).
2 Esdras.audience: Jews after 70 AD wrestling with theodicy; later expanded for Christian readers.
2 Esdras.date: Jewish core c. 100 AD; Christian additions c. 2nd–3rd century AD.

Didache.author: Anonymous (the title means "Teaching of the Twelve Apostles").
Didache.audience: Early Christian assemblies — a brief manual on ethics, baptism, eucharist, and traveling teachers.

Gospel of Thomas.author: Anonymous; the incipit attributes the sayings collection to "Didymos Judas Thomas." Surviving in full only in a 4th-century Coptic translation from Nag Hammadi (NHC II,2), with three Greek fragments from Oxyrhynchus.
Gospel of Thomas.audience: A Christian readership shaped by Syrian wisdom and proto-Gnostic thought, oriented to esoteric self-knowledge in Jesus' sayings.
Gospel of Thomas.date: Greek original likely c. 50–140 AD; Coptic manuscript c. 340 AD.
Gospel of Thomas.summary: The Gospel of Thomas is a collection of sayings attributed to Jesus. It has no continuous story and repeatedly calls readers to discover the meaning of the sayings.

Gospel of Truth.author: Anonymous; widely attributed to Valentinus or his school.
Gospel of Truth.audience: Christian readers within the Valentinian Gnostic movement.
Gospel of Truth.date: c. mid-2nd century AD; preserved at Nag Hammadi.

Jubilees.author: Anonymous; presented as a Sinai revelation to Moses.
Jubilees.audience: Jewish communities (likely the same milieu as Qumran) committed to a 364-day solar calendar and strict halakha.
Jubilees.date: c. mid-2nd century BC; preserved in full in Ge'ez (Ethiopic).

Psalms of Solomon.author: Anonymous; pseudonymously attributed to Solomon.
Psalms of Solomon.audience: Pious Jews in Jerusalem reacting to Pompey's conquest in 63 BC.

Shepherd of Hermas.author: Hermas, a Christian living in Rome.
Shepherd of Hermas.audience: The Christian assembly in Rome — a moral and apocalyptic prophecy on repentance.

Thunder, Perfect Mind.author: Anonymous.
Thunder, Perfect Mind.audience: A Greco-Egyptian wisdom or Gnostic readership; gendered self-revelation poem in the voice of a divine female figure.
Thunder, Perfect Mind.date: Likely c. 1st–2nd century AD; preserved at Nag Hammadi (NHC VI,2).

Testament of Reuben.author: Anonymous; part of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, presented as the deathbed speeches of Jacob's sons.
Testament of Reuben.audience: Jewish (and later Christian) readers learning ethics from the patriarchs' confessions.
Testament of Reuben.date: Pre-Christian Jewish core c. 2nd century BC; Christian editorial layer c. 1st–2nd century AD.

Testament of Simeon.author: Anonymous; part of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs.
Testament of Simeon.date: c. 2nd century BC Jewish core; Christian editing c. 1st–2nd century AD.

Testament of Levi.author: Anonymous; part of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs.
Testament of Levi.audience: Jewish (and later Christian) readers; especially priestly-interested communities.
Testament of Levi.date: c. 2nd century BC Jewish core; Christian editing c. 1st–2nd century AD.

Testament of Judah.author: Anonymous; part of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs.
Testament of Judah.date: c. 2nd century BC Jewish core; Christian editing c. 1st–2nd century AD.

Testament of Issachar.author: Anonymous; part of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs.
Testament of Issachar.date: c. 2nd century BC Jewish core; Christian editing c. 1st–2nd century AD.

Testament of Zebulun.author: Anonymous; part of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs.
Testament of Zebulun.date: c. 2nd century BC Jewish core; Christian editing c. 1st–2nd century AD.

Testament of Dan.author: Anonymous; part of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs.
Testament of Dan.date: c. 2nd century BC Jewish core; Christian editing c. 1st–2nd century AD.

Testament of Naphtali.author: Anonymous; part of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs.
Testament of Naphtali.date: c. 2nd century BC Jewish core; Christian editing c. 1st–2nd century AD.

Testament of Gad.author: Anonymous; part of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs.
Testament of Gad.date: c. 2nd century BC Jewish core; Christian editing c. 1st–2nd century AD.

Testament of Asher.author: Anonymous; part of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs.
Testament of Asher.date: c. 2nd century BC Jewish core; Christian editing c. 1st–2nd century AD.

Testament of Joseph.author: Anonymous; part of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs.
Testament of Joseph.date: c. 2nd century BC Jewish core; Christian editing c. 1st–2nd century AD.

Testament of Benjamin.author: Anonymous; part of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs.
Testament of Benjamin.date: c. 2nd century BC Jewish core; Christian editing c. 1st–2nd century AD.

Gospel of Philip.author: Anonymous. The title appears in the manuscript's closing subscription, but the work does not identify Philip as its writer. The sole surviving copy is the Coptic text of Nag Hammadi Codex II,3.
Gospel of Philip.audience: An early Christian community familiar with Valentinian-style sacramental instruction, especially baptism, anointing, Eucharist, redemption, resurrection, and bridal-chamber imagery.
Gospel of Philip.date: Commonly dated to the late 2nd or early 3rd century AD; preserved in a 4th-century Coptic manuscript translated from an earlier Greek form.

Gospel of Mary.author: Anonymous. The work presents Mary as a recipient and interpreter of Jesus' revelation, but it does not claim that Mary wrote the surviving gospel.
Gospel of Mary.audience: Early Christian readers wrestling with revelation, spiritual ascent, apostolic authority, and the legitimacy of Mary's teaching among Jesus' disciples.
Gospel of Mary.date: Usually dated to the 2nd century AD; Greek fragments survive from the 3rd century, and the principal Coptic witness is preserved in the 5th-century Berlin Codex 8502.

Treatise on the Resurrection.author: Anonymous. The work is framed as a teacher's letter to a pupil named Rheginos; neither the teacher nor Rheginos can be identified securely.
Treatise on the Resurrection.audience: Christians seeking instruction about resurrection, especially readers weighing bodily, spiritual, and present participation in resurrection life.
Treatise on the Resurrection.date: Usually placed in the late 2nd century AD (often c. 170–200); preserved in a 4th-century Coptic copy of an earlier Greek work.

Dialogue of the Savior.author: Anonymous. The dialogue places revelatory teaching on Jesus' lips in conversation with Judas, Matthew, and Mary, but it does not identify its compiler.
Dialogue of the Savior.audience: An early Christian circle interested in private revelation, discipleship, self-knowledge, prayer, and ascetic preparation for salvation.
Dialogue of the Savior.date: Commonly assigned to the 2nd century AD, though its compositional layers and exact date remain disputed; preserved in a 4th-century Coptic manuscript.

Exegesis on the Soul.author: Anonymous. The author is a Christian homilist who rereads biblical and Greek literary images as an allegory of the soul's fall, repentance, and restoration.
Exegesis on the Soul.audience: Christians familiar with Scripture and moral exhortation who were being called from disordered desire to repentance and reunion with the divine.
Exegesis on the Soul.date: Generally dated to the late 2nd or early 3rd century AD; preserved in a 4th-century Coptic translation from Greek.

Book of Thomas the Contender.author: Anonymous. Its closing title associates the work with Judas Thomas and names Mathaias as recorder, but these are literary attributions rather than verifiable authorship claims.
Book of Thomas the Contender.audience: Ascetically inclined Christians urged to seek self-knowledge, resist bodily passions, and understand Jesus' private instruction to Thomas.
Book of Thomas the Contender.date: Often dated to the late 2nd or early 3rd century AD, possibly in a Syrian Christian setting; preserved in a 4th-century Coptic manuscript.

Tripartite Tractate.author: Anonymous. The author was a highly educated Valentinian Christian theologian; no secure identification with a named teacher is possible.
Tripartite Tractate.audience: A Valentinian Christian community receiving sustained instruction about God, the aeons, creation, Christ, the church, salvation, and final restoration.
Tripartite Tractate.date: Usually dated to the 3rd century AD, with some arguments favoring its latter half; preserved in the 4th-century Jung Codex in Coptic.

Apocryphon of John.author: Anonymous. The work pseudonymously presents a revelation of the risen Jesus to John the son of Zebedee and survives in more than one ancient recension.
Apocryphon of John.audience: Christians in a Sethian or closely related revelatory tradition seeking an account of the divine realm, creation, human identity, and liberation from hostile rulers.
Apocryphon of John.date: An early form likely circulated in the 2nd century AD; the surviving Coptic witnesses, preserving shorter and longer recensions, date from the 4th and 5th centuries.

Hypostasis of the Archons.author: Anonymous. The author interprets Genesis through a revelatory myth about the archons; the work cannot be assigned securely to a named teacher.
Hypostasis of the Archons.audience: Christians in a Sethian or related milieu who read Genesis as a conflict between ignorant cosmic rulers, divine wisdom, and humanity's spiritual origin.
Hypostasis of the Archons.date: Commonly placed in the 3rd century AD; preserved in a 4th-century Coptic copy in Nag Hammadi Codex II.

On the Origin of the World.display_name: On the Origin of the World
On the Origin of the World.author: Anonymous. The work combines and revises several Jewish, Christian, Platonic, and mythological traditions without naming its compiler.
On the Origin of the World.audience: Readers in a Gnosticizing Christian environment seeking a counter-history of creation, the cosmic rulers, Sophia, Adam and Eve, and the world's final destiny.
On the Origin of the World.date: Usually dated to the 3rd century AD, though earlier materials may underlie it; preserved principally in 4th-century Coptic witnesses.

Sophia of Jesus Christ.author: Anonymous. The author adapts material also known from Eugnostos into a post-resurrection dialogue between Jesus and his disciples.
Sophia of Jesus Christ.audience: Christians interested in revealed wisdom about the transcendent God, the ordering of the heavenly world, and the soul's origin and salvation.
Sophia of Jesus Christ.date: Often dated to the late 2nd or 3rd century AD; preserved in Coptic copies from Nag Hammadi and the Berlin Codex.

Gospel of the Egyptians.author: Anonymous. This Nag Hammadi work, also called the Holy Book of the Great Invisible Spirit, is distinct from the earlier Greek Gospel of the Egyptians known only through quotations.
Gospel of the Egyptians.audience: A Sethian Christian community using dense myth, sacred names, baptismal imagery, and hymnic praise to articulate spiritual identity and deliverance.
Gospel of the Egyptians.date: Usually assigned to the 2nd or 3rd century AD; two Coptic copies survive in 4th-century Nag Hammadi codices.

Letter of Peter to Philip.author: Anonymous. The brief opening letter and ensuing revelation are pseudonymously attributed to Peter and Philip rather than securely written by either apostle.
Letter of Peter to Philip.audience: Christians seeking apostolic authorization for teaching about the Savior, hostile powers, suffering, mission, and the restoration of the disciples.
Letter of Peter to Philip.date: Commonly dated to the late 2nd or early 3rd century AD; preserved in a 4th-century Nag Hammadi copy and a later Coptic witness.

Gospel of Judas.author: Anonymous. The title attributes the narrative to Judas, but the work does not establish Judas Iscariot as its historical author.
Gospel of Judas.audience: A Christian group critical of rival sacrificial and ecclesial practices, using revelatory dialogue and Sethian-type cosmology to reinterpret Judas and Jesus' death.
Gospel of Judas.date: Usually dated to the mid- or late 2nd century AD; Irenaeus knew a Gospel of Judas by c. 180, and the surviving Coptic copy is probably 3rd or 4th century.

Protoevangelium of James.author: Anonymous. The narrator claims to be James, but the work is pseudonymous and was not written by James the brother of Jesus.
Protoevangelium of James.audience: Christians interested in Mary's birth and upbringing, her perpetual purity, Jesus' nativity, and narrative answers to questions left open by Matthew and Luke.
Protoevangelium of James.date: Generally dated to the latter half of the 2nd century AD; it survives in numerous later Greek manuscripts and ancient translations.

Infancy Gospel of Thomas.author: Anonymous. Its earliest recoverable form does not name an author; attribution to Thomas belongs to later manuscript titles and transmission.
Infancy Gospel of Thomas.audience: Christians curious about Jesus' childhood and how divine power, discipline, learning, and maturation might be narrated before the canonical Gospel accounts begin.
Infancy Gospel of Thomas.date: Usually traced to the 2nd century AD, but the text survives in several substantially different Greek recensions and early translations.

Acts of Paul and Thecla.author: Anonymous. It is an episode from the larger Acts of Paul; an ancient report that a presbyter composed the Acts cannot securely identify the author.
Acts of Paul and Thecla.audience: Christians drawn to stories of apostolic preaching, celibacy, baptism, martyr-like endurance, and a woman's authority to teach and bear witness.
Acts of Paul and Thecla.date: Composed in the 2nd century AD, probably in its latter half; it circulated both within the Acts of Paul and as an independent work.

Gospel of Peter.author: Anonymous. The surviving narrative speaks in Peter's voice and was transmitted under his name, but it is not regarded as a work of the historical apostle.
Gospel of Peter.audience: Early Christians interested in an expanded passion-and-resurrection narrative, probably within communities where Petrine authority carried special weight.
Gospel of Peter.date: Usually dated to the 2nd century AD; the principal surviving Greek fragment comes from a much later manuscript found at Akhmim.

2 Clement.author: Anonymous. Despite its traditional title, this is an early Christian homily rather than a second letter by Clement of Rome.
2 Clement.audience: A Christian assembly exhorted to repentance, moral consistency, care for the vulnerable, and faithful endurance in hope of resurrection and judgment.
2 Clement.date: Usually dated to the first half or middle of the 2nd century AD (approximately c. 100–160); its place of composition is uncertain.

Epistle of Barnabas.author: Anonymous. The work was traditionally associated with Paul's companion Barnabas, but modern scholarship does not accept that attribution.
Epistle of Barnabas.audience: Gentile Christians being taught to claim Israel's Scriptures through christological and allegorical interpretation while distinguishing their covenant identity from Jewish practice.
Epistle of Barnabas.date: Commonly dated between the destruction of the Jerusalem temple in AD 70 and the early 2nd century, often c. 80–130.

Letters of Ignatius.author: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, for the seven letters of the commonly accepted middle recension; later expanded and pseudonymous Ignatian letters are outside this collection.
Letters of Ignatius.audience: Christian assemblies in Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles, Rome, Philadelphia, and Smyrna, together with Polycarp, addressed during Ignatius's journey toward martyrdom.
Letters of Ignatius.date: Usually dated to the early 2nd century AD, commonly c. 105–117, though the precise chronology of Ignatius's journey remains debated.

Polycarp to the Philippians.author: Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna. Some scholars understand the received text as combining material sent at more than one moment.
Polycarp to the Philippians.audience: The Christian assembly at Philippi, which requested Ignatius's letters and received counsel on faith, conduct, leadership, money, and perseverance.
Polycarp to the Philippians.date: Early to mid-2nd century AD; at least part is closely connected with Ignatius's journey, while proposals for a composite letter allow a somewhat later section.

Martyrdom of Polycarp.author: Anonymous members of the church in Smyrna, writing in the community's name; the closing transmission notes reflect later copying and circulation.
Martyrdom of Polycarp.audience: The church at Philomelium and the wider Christian communion, offered an account of Polycarp's arrest, trial, death, and exemplary endurance.
Martyrdom of Polycarp.date: Written after Polycarp's death, usually placed in the mid- or later 2nd century AD; both the martyrdom's exact year and the document's final form are debated.

Epistle to Diognetus.author: Anonymous. The writer calls himself a disciple or learner, but neither he nor the addressed Diognetus can be identified securely.
Epistle to Diognetus.audience: An educated non-Christian inquirer—and readers like him—asking about Christian worship, ethics, social identity, love, and the apparent newness of the faith.
Epistle to Diognetus.date: Often dated to the late 2nd or early 3rd century AD, though proposals vary widely; the final two chapters may come from a different work.

Fragments of Papias.author: Papias, bishop of Hierapolis, for the lost five-book Expositions of the Sayings of the Lord; the surviving collection consists of quotations and reports preserved by later authors.
Fragments of Papias.audience: Early Christians seeking remembered teachings about Jesus and the apostles, gathered through named chains of oral testimony and interpretation.
Fragments of Papias.date: Papias's work is usually dated to the early 2nd century AD, often c. 110–130; the surviving fragments occur in authors writing from the 2nd century onward.
